questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `p` points to `i` and `q` points to `p`, so `**q = 3` writes into `i`. The last assignment wins.
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int i{ 5 }; int* p{ &i }; *p = -7; int** q{ &p }; **q = 3; std::cout << i << "\n"; }

questions.question: Does this compile?
choices: No: `a` itself is const and can't be reassigned
No: you can't take the address of `i`
questions.explanation: `int * const a` is a **constant pointer** to a modifiable int: `*a = 2` is fine, but `a = &j` isn't.
questions.code: int main() { int i{ 1 }, j{ 2 }; int * const a{ &i }; *a = 2; a = &j; return i; }

questions.question: In `int const * p`, what is constant?
questions.explanation: Read right to left: *p is a pointer to a const int*. `int const *` is the same as `const int *`.

questions.question: Which of these is **not** an lvalue (with `int i; int* p;`)?
questions.explanation: `i++` returns a copy of the *old* value, a temporary. `++i` and `i = 2` return `i` itself, and `*p` designates the object pointed to (slide 69).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `ri` is an alias of `i`. `ri = j` assigns **j's value** to `i`; it doesn't rebind the reference. A reference can never be re-seated.
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int i{ 3 }; int& ri{ i }; int j{ 7 }; ri = j; std::cout << i << " " << ri << "\n"; }

questions.question: Does this compile?
choices: No: a non-const lvalue reference can't bind to a temporary
questions.explanation: `j + 2` is an rvalue, and `int&` binds only to lvalues. Use `const int&` (or `int&&`) to accept temporaries.
questions.code:
void f(int& i) { i = 3; }
int main() { int j{ 8 }; f(j + 2); return j; }

questions.question: Is there undefined behaviour?
choices: Yes: the pointer is used after `delete`
questions.explanation: After `delete p`, the memory is released and `*p` is a **use after free**: undefined behaviour, which ASan reports.
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { int* p = new int{ 5 }; delete p; std::cout << *p << "\n"; }

questions.question: On a 64-bit machine, what does this print?
questions.explanation: `sizeof(tab)` is the size of the whole array (10 × 4 bytes). Passed to `f`, the array **decays** to a pointer, and `sizeof` gives the size of the pointer (8).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `v1{ 10 }` uses the **initializer-list** constructor: one element, 10. `v2( 10 )` creates 10 zero elements. Hence slide 80's warning: *Parenthèses !*

questions.question: Which storage duration has **no default initialisation** and is released at the end of the enclosing block?
questions.explanation: Automatic variables (ordinary locals) are created when their definition is reached and destroyed at the end of the block. Only static storage is zero-initialised by default (slides 66–68).

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `p2 - p1` is measured in **elements**, not bytes (slide 77).
questions.code:
#include <iostream>
int main() { double tab[10]; double* p1{ &tab[2] }; double* p2{ &tab[5] }; std::cout << p2 - p1 << "\n"; }

questions.question: Is there undefined behaviour?
choices: Only if the vector is empty
questions.explanation: `operator[]` does **not** check the index, so `v[3]` on a 3-element vector is out of bounds. `v.at(3)` would throw `std::out_of_range` instead.
